explanations.explanation: Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, has two projects on his mind. One is a house for the Name of the LORD, and the other is a royal palace for himself. The verse says he "purposed" to build both. So palace is the word, and I'd say that's a pretty big weekend of building.

A fortress sounds like a king thing, so I see why you grabbed it. But the verse says Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, planned a royal palace for himself. Nothing in it mentions a fortress. Palace is the word, friend.

A garden would be a lovely thing to have, but it isn't in this verse. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, planned a house for the Name of the LORD and a royal palace for himself. Palace is the word that fits the blank.

Solomon, David's son, reminds Hiram, king of Tyre, of the favor he did for David before. Hiram sent David cedars so David could build himself a house to live in. Now Solomon is asking for the same kind of help. When a plan worked once, it makes sense to go back to the same lumberyard.

Horses make a good gift, but that's not what Hiram, king of Tyre, sent. Solomon says Hiram sent his father David cedars to build himself a house to live in. Cedars are wood for building. So no horses in this one, friend.

Silver comes up later in Solomon's message, where he asks Hiram, king of Tyre, for a craftsman skilled in working with it. But in this verse Solomon is talking about what Hiram once did for his father David. Hiram sent David cedars to build himself a house to live in. Solomon wants that same help again.

Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, tells Hiram the burnt offerings will be made every morning and evening. They'll also be made on the Sabbaths, New Moons and appointed feasts of the LORD. That's a steady rhythm, twice a day.

Once a year would be a pretty light schedule, but that's not what Solomon says. He tells Hiram, king of Tyre, the burnt offerings are for every morning and evening. They're also for the Sabbaths, New Moons and appointed feasts of the LORD. So this is a daily rhythm, friend, not a yearly one.

Harvest time isn't named here. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, tells Hiram the burnt offerings will be made every morning and evening. He adds the Sabbaths, New Moons and appointed feasts of the LORD. That's a lot more often than one season.

Solomon finishes his list of what the house is for with these words to Hiram, king of Tyre: "This is ordained for Israel forever." The incense, the showbread and the offerings are not a one-time event. They're meant to keep going. Solomon wants Hiram to know what he's helping build.

This one is actually true. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, ends his list to Hiram, king of Tyre, with these words: "This is ordained for Israel forever." So the incense, showbread and offerings are meant to continue and not stop. Easy one to second-guess, friend.

explanations.answer: Because God is greater than all gods
explanations.explanation: Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, doesn't brag about the building or his own power. He tells Hiram the house will be great, "…for our God is greater than all gods." The greatness comes from who the house is for. That's the right place to put it.

explanations.answer: Because the kings around him had temples
explanations.explanation: Solomon never points to other kings or their temples. He tells Hiram, king of Tyre, the house will be great, "…for our God is greater than all gods." The reason isn't about keeping up with the neighbors. It's about who God is.

explanations.answer: Because Israel is stronger than Tyre
explanations.explanation: That would be a strange thing to say to Hiram, king of Tyre, when you're asking him for cedar. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, never compares the two nations. He says the house will be great, "…for our God is greater than all gods." His reason is God, not Israel's strength.

explanations.answer: Even the highest heavens cannot contain Him
explanations.explanation: Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, asks, "But who is able to build a house for Him, since the heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain Him?" If the highest heavens can't hold God, no building can either. He knows it's a big job and an even bigger God. And he's humble about it.

explanations.answer: No one on earth has enough gold for it
explanations.explanation: Gold does come up in this passage, since Solomon wants a craftsman who can work with it. But gold isn't his reason here. He says, "…since the heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain Him?" The problem is how big God is, not how little money there is.

explanations.answer: The whole land of Israel is too small
explanations.explanation: Solomon doesn't say anything about the size of Israel. His reason is bigger than any land. He says, "…since the heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain Him?" If the highest heavens can't contain God, that settles it.

Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, asks Hiram, king of Tyre, to send "…a craftsman skilled in engraving…" He wants someone who can work with gold, silver, bronze, iron, and purple, crimson and blue yarn. That's a long list for one person. Solomon is shopping for real talent.

This one is true. In verse 7, Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, asks Hiram, king of Tyre, to send "…a craftsman skilled in engraving…" He also wants that craftsman to work with gold, silver, bronze, iron and colored yarn. So the engraver is on the order, friend.

Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, says the craftsman from Tyre will work with his craftsmen "…in Judah and Jerusalem…" He adds that his father David provided them. So the visiting expert joins a team that's already in place. Nobody has to work alone.

Bethel isn't named in this verse. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, says the craftsman from Tyre will work with his craftsmen in Judah and Jerusalem. His father David provided those craftsmen. Jerusalem is the one that fits the blank.

Hebron didn't make the guest list for this verse, friend. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, says the craftsman from Tyre will work with his own craftsmen in Judah and Jerusalem. Those are the craftsmen his father David provided. Jerusalem is what goes in the blank.

Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, doesn't say that. He tells Hiram, king of Tyre, "…my servants will work with yours" The plan is for both crews to work together preparing timber. So Hiram's men won't be left to do it all alone.

The answer is false, and that's the right call. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, tells Hiram, king of Tyre, "…my servants will work with yours" The two crews are meant to work side by side. Solomon is asking for teamwork, not a hand-off.

explanations.answer: Wheat and barley and wine and oil
explanations.explanation: Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, promises Hiram's woodcutters 20,000 cors of ground wheat, 20,000 cors of barley, 20,000 baths of wine and 20,000 baths of olive oil. So the pay comes in grain, wine and oil, and there's plenty of it. Solomon plans to pay for what he asks.

explanations.answer: Silver and gold and bronze and iron
explanations.explanation: Those metals are in this passage, but not as the woodcutters' pay. In verse 7, Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, mentions them as materials the craftsman works with. The pay for Hiram's woodcutters is 20,000 each of ground wheat, barley, wine and olive oil. That's what's in the pay envelope.

explanations.answer: Horses and chariots and carts and mules
explanations.explanation: None of those show up in Solomon's offer. He, David's son and Israel's king, promises Hiram's woodcutters 20,000 cors of ground wheat, 20,000 cors of barley, 20,000 baths of wine and 20,000 baths of olive oil. That's wheat, barley, wine and oil. No stable needed.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD loves His people
explanations.explanation: Hiram, king of Tyre, writes back to Solomon, David's son and Israel's king: "Because the LORD loves His people, He has set you over them as king." Hiram points to the LORD's love for His people and nothing else. Not bad for the first lines of a business letter.

explanations.answer: Because David asked the LORD to
explanations.explanation: Hiram, king of Tyre, doesn't mention David asking for anything in this line. He writes to Solomon, David's son and Israel's king: "Because the LORD loves His people, He has set you over them as king." The reason Hiram gives is the LORD's love for His people.

explanations.answer: Because Solomon was the oldest son
explanations.explanation: Hiram, king of Tyre, says nothing about birth order. He writes to Solomon, David's son and Israel's king: "Because the LORD loves His people, He has set you over them as king." That's the whole reason he gives.

Hiram, king of Tyre, writes, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who made the heavens and the earth! He has given King David a wise son with insight and understanding…" That wise son is Solomon, who is getting the letter. Hiram put it in writing, friend. That's a nice thing to find in the mail.

This one is true. Hiram, king of Tyre, writes, "He has given King David a wise son with insight and understanding…" The wise son is Solomon, who receives the letter. So Hiram does say it, right there in verse 12.

Hiram, king of Tyre, says Huram-abi, the craftsman he's sending, is "…the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan…" His father is a man of Tyre. So his mother comes from the daughters of Dan, and his father is from Tyre.

Levi? LEVI? Friend, Levi never shows up in Hiram's letter. Not once. I went looking for it like the last crumb at the bottom of the cookie box, and all I found was empty cardboard. Hiram, king of Tyre, says Huram-abi, the craftsman he's sending, is the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan, and his father is a man of Tyre. So the answer is Dan.

This one is false. Hiram, king of Tyre, says Huram-abi is skilled in work with gold and silver, bronze and iron, stone and wood, purple, blue and crimson yarn, and fine linen. He adds that Huram-abi is experienced in every kind of engraving. Metal is only the start of his skills.

Hiram, king of Tyre, describes Huram-abi as skilled in gold, silver, bronze and iron. But the list keeps going: stone, wood, colored yarn and fine linen. He can also execute any design he's given. That resume would not fit on one page.

explanations.answer: Float them as rafts by sea
explanations.explanation: Hiram, king of Tyre, says, "We will cut logs from Lebanon, as many as you need, and we will float them to you as rafts by sea down to Joppa." So the logs ride the water instead of a road. I think that beats carrying them one at a time. Solomon can take them up to Jerusalem from there.

explanations.answer: Haul them on carts over land
explanations.explanation: Carts aren't in Hiram's plan. Hiram, king of Tyre, says his men will cut the logs in Lebanon and float them as rafts by sea. They're headed down to Joppa. After that, Solomon can take them up to Jerusalem.

explanations.answer: Carry them on camels through the hills
explanations.explanation: Camels don't show up in Hiram's letter. Hiram, king of Tyre, says, "…we will float them to you as rafts by sea down to Joppa." The sea does the hauling. After that, Solomon can take the logs up to Jerusalem.
Hiram, king of Tyre, says his men will float the logs as rafts by sea "…down to Joppa." From there, Solomon can take them up to Jerusalem. So Joppa is where the sea trip ends and the next leg begins.
Tarshish isn't in Hiram's letter. Hiram, king of Tyre, says the log rafts will float by sea down to Joppa. After that, Solomon can take the logs up to Jerusalem. Joppa is the port in this plan.

Ezion-geber doesn't appear in this letter. Hiram, king of Tyre, says his men will float the logs as rafts by sea down to Joppa. Then Solomon can take them up to Jerusalem. Joppa is where the rafts land, friend.
